claims.text: Group disparate outcomes in employment can persist even when hiring decisions strictly adhere to input-output metrics of individual fairness.
Imposing a statistical parity constraint on hiring in a Temporary Labor Market (TLM) induces a unique, stable, and symmetric steady-state equilibrium across groups.
The statistical parity constraint in the Temporary Labor Market (TLM) does not need to be permanent to maintain long-term group equality.
Under unsaturated demand for skilled workers, the symmetric steady-state equilibrium resulting from a TLM fairness constraint Pareto-dominates equilibria under group-blind hiring strategies.

Under unsaturated demand for skilled workers, the symmetric steady-state equilibrium resulting from a TLM fairness constraint Pareto-dominates equilibria under statistical discriminatory hiring strategies.
Procedural fairness checks restricted strictly to the hiring decision are insufficient to resolve structural development bias and investment disparities.

evidence.description: Mathematical formulation demonstrating that cyclic equilibrium ensures local procedural fairness with respect to investment choices while preserving global disparate outcomes.
Proof of Theorem 3.1 showing that under TLM statistical parity hiring, the dynamic mapping of group outcomes is a contraction map converging to a unique symmetric fixed point.
Derivation showing that once initial group equality is restored, statistical parity of hired workers naturally results from firms' optimal hiring strategies without active enforcement.

Proof of Theorem 3.2 showing that group-blind hiring creates inefficiently high effective ability thresholds for disadvantaged groups, whereas TLM constrained hiring increases disadvantaged group employment without harming the favored group.
Proof of Theorem 3.2 demonstrating that self-confirming asymmetric equilibria under statistical discrimination produce lost efficiency that is recovered under statistical parity hiring.
Theoretical analysis showing that worker investments are strategic choices driven by group reputational externalities, which static input-output fairness metrics treat as fixed inputs.

methodologies.name: Dynamic reputational dual labor market game model
methodologies.description: A dynamic game-theoretic model partitioning the labor market into a Temporary Labor Market (TLM) constrained by statistical parity and a Permanent Labor Market (PLM) governed by relational reputational contracts.
conditions: Two demographic groups with identical underlying intrinsic ability distributions F(theta)
TLM firms constrained to enforce statistical parity among hired workers
PLM hiring based on individual performance histories (reputation metrics)
Unsaturated demand for skilled workers in PLM (wage w = w_bar)

limitations.text: Employment outcomes along the transition path toward symmetric equilibrium are not guaranteed to satisfy individual or group fairness metrics.
The model simplifies real-world labor pipelines into discrete pre-TLM, TLM, and PLM stages, omitting real-world structural heterogeneity and complex social dynamics.
Existing static algorithmic fairness definitions evaluate decision functions as domain-general input-output mappings, ignoring strategic agent incentives and dynamic feedback loops in labor markets.

future_work.text: Determine how algorithmic systems sifting through historical worker data in PLM settings should incorporate group membership considerations.
Conduct theoretical and empirical cost and efficiency evaluations of alternative intervention types across different stages of the social and economic pipeline.
